title: Prepositions and preposition phrases
description: See why prepositions are phrase heads, how their complements and modifiers work, and how English uses them for place, time, grammar and style.
example: The keys were left just inside the drawer, behind a pile of old photographs.

key_terms.definition: A word that heads a preposition phrase and typically takes a complement.
A phrase headed by a preposition, with an optional complement and optional modifiers.
A dependent licensed by the head, such as the drawer in inside the drawer.
A dependent that adds information without being required by the head.
A preposition used without a complement, such as outside in She is outside.
The use of a preposition without its complement in the normal post-head position, as in What are you looking at?
Fronting a preposition together with its complement, as in To whom are you speaking?
A preposition selected by a grammatical construction rather than chosen for its independent meaning.
An NP related to a head through a preposition rather than directly.
The NP complement of a transitive preposition, as in the garden in in the garden.
A complement related to a predicand, as in as treasurer.
A modifier in clause structure, often realised by a PP.
The entity whose location or movement is specified in a spatial relation.
The reference point or area relative to which a trajector is located.
The starting point of a path or change of location, often marked by from or off.
The endpoint of a path or change of location, often marked by to or into.
A static spatial relation, often marked by at, on or in.
An expression whose meaning is not fully predictable from its parts.
A fixed expression with limited internal variation, often headed by a preposition.
A clause functioning as the complement of a preposition or other head.
A marker introducing a subordinate clause, such as whether, if or that.
A preposition that takes an object NP complement.
Movement of a constituent to a position before the nucleus clause.
A detached element related to an anchor without being a syntactic dependent.

intro: Ask a room of students what a preposition is and someone will offer *in*, *on*, *under* — little words that say where or when. That list is a reasonable start, and almost everything interesting about the category lies in how quickly it breaks down. *In* in *She stayed in* has no noun after it at all. *Because* in *Because it rained* carries a whole clause. *From behind the curtain* puts one preposition phrase inside another. Small words, yes; simple, no.

The change of perspective is to treat a preposition as a head. It projects a phrase, takes a complement, tolerates modifiers, and can stand alone when nothing needs saying. Once *because* and *outside* and *downstairs* count as heads of phrases, the class grows well beyond the traditional short list, and its membership stops looking arbitrary. What matters is the structure a word builds, not the size of the word itself.

From there the account works outward: membership first, then the complements and modifiers a preposition can carry, then the curious business of stranding — the preposition left behind when its complement moves to the front. Idioms, phrase functions, grammaticised uses, spatial and temporal meaning, and finally the stylistic question of when to strand and when to front.

blocks.text: *Max sent a photograph of his new house to his parents.* Two phrases in that clause are doing work no single word could do: *of his new house* picks out which photograph, *to his parents* says where it went. Each begins with a preposition, and each preposition relates what follows to something already established — *of* ties the house to the photograph, *to* ties the parents to the sending.

*From behind the curtain* puts a PP inside a PP; *on whether we should call the police* puts an interrogative clause after the preposition; *until recently* puts an adverb phrase there. The relation survives when the complement is not a noun phrase at all. This is the same head–complement pattern that links a verb to its object, and it is what makes the preposition a head rather than a mere linker. The filler varies; the structure does not.

Modification follows from the same analysis. In *just inside the penalty area*, *just* narrows a location that *inside* has already fixed; in *two years after their divorce*, the measure phrase sets a distance in time. Neither modifier is selected by the head, so neither is a complement. Drop them and the phrase survives, thinner but intact.

sections.title: Who belongs to the preposition category

blocks.text: *Of*, *to*, *in*, *on*, *at*, *by*, *for*, *with*, *from*, *between*: the familiar core, every one of them taking a noun phrase and building a phrase that slots into a clause as complement or adjunct. Around that core sit words doing the same structural work while looking less like prepositions — *after* with a clause, *outside* with no complement, *provided* with a condition attached. Membership is decided by the work, not the appearance.

*Because it rained* is a phrase headed by *because* whose complement is a finite clause, exactly parallel to *in the garden*. Most of what older grammars call subordinating conjunctions are prepositions here. The traditional label tracks meaning and clause-linking; the analysis tracks heads and complements, and the second test is the one that groups words together. Three items stay outside the class — *whether*, interrogative *if*, and the *that* which introduces clauses — because they mark a clause without heading a phrase.

*She is outside.* Nothing follows the preposition, and the sentence is complete. *I haven’t seen her since* and *put it downstairs* show the same intransitive use. A missing complement does not change the category, any more than a missing object turns a verb into something else; that is why *outside* counts as a preposition in *They are outside* while *locally*, an adverb, cannot take its place.

New prepositions do appear, but English has no productive suffix or compounding pattern that manufactures them, so the list grows slowly and by borrowing rather than by rule. The class is relatively closed. Closure does not mean uniformity: many members have grammaticised uses in which a construction selects the preposition and its spatial or temporal meaning fades. The *by* of the passive, the *of* in *the destruction of the city*, the *to* in *give it to Kim* are chosen by grammar, not by the speaker’s picture of the scene.

blocks.text: *Ahead of the ship, there was a small island* locates the island and says nothing about anyone’s state of mind. Replace the PP with an adjective phrase and the sentence commits itself: *Tired of the ship, the captain saw an island* attributes the tiredness to the captain. A fronted AdjP of that kind is predicative and needs a predicand; a PP in the same slot is a plain adjunct, free of the commitment.

*Go*, *went*, *gone*: verbs mark tense by inflection. *In*, *into*, *inside*: prepositions do not. Complementation is a softer test. Both categories take objects, and a PP can be fronted with its object intact — *the knife with which she cut it* — while a verb cannot drag its object forward the same way.

*I put it in the drawer* cannot shrink to *I put it*; the locative is required, and *Jill is in the office* resists *Jill is* for the same reason. An *-ly* adverb does not fill that slot. *Jill is locally* does not give *be* the complement it needs, which is why adverbs serve as complements only in restricted cases while many prepositions head obligatory ones.

Some words sit on the boundary. *Worth* takes a noun phrase complement like a preposition — *worth the effort* — but predicates and modifies like an adjective, so the label depends on which part of the pattern you weight. *Owing* is a preposition in *owing to the weather* and a participle in *owing money to the bank*. *Opposite* goes both ways. No single resemblance settles these cases; the whole distribution does.

blocks.text: *In the garden*, *to Paris*, *with my sister*. The default shape is a preposition plus a noun phrase, and the noun phrase is the object of the preposition, which makes the preposition transitive in the ordinary sense. *In* is transitive in *She stayed in the house* and intransitive in *She stayed in*, with no change in the word itself.

Beyond the noun phrase the range widens. *From* takes a PP in *from behind the curtain*; *until* takes an adverb phrase in *until recently*. Both are ordinary head–complement structures with unusual fillers, and the complement type belongs to the head’s lexical entry as much as it does for a verb.

*I regard their behaviour as outrageous.* The adjective phrase after *as* describes the behaviour, not the regarding, so it is a predicative complement and *as* is the preposition that licenses it. *For* does similar work after *take* and *pass*: *I took him for harmless*, *He passed for dead*. Most other prepositions take ordinary objects, and the object/predicative line inside a PP is the same line that runs through verb complementation.

*Apart from Jill* and *since before the war* look alike and are not. In the first, *apart* selects *from*; the two form a fixed combination. In the second, *since* does not select *before* — *before* makes its own contribution, which is why *since after the war* contrasts with it. Specified versus unspecified prepositions: that is the distinction at work.

sections.title: Modification and the shape of PPs

blocks.text: *Two years after their divorce* and *just inside the penalty area* both place something before the preposition, but the somethings do different work. The measure phrase sets a distance in time; the focus adverb narrows a location. *Very much in control* adds degree, *right under the bed* adds emphasis. Where the modifier sits depends on what it takes scope over.

*Right* and *straight* are unusually choosy. They modify spatial and temporal prepositions — *right under the bed*, *straight upstairs* — and refuse verbs, adjectives and adverbs. The choosiness is a test. If *right* can stand in front of a word, that word is probably heading a PP, which is how *in*, *inside* and *upstairs* separate themselves from adverbs of identical shape.

PPs nest productively. *From behind the curtain*, *out of the box*, *next to her sister*: in each, a PP sits inside a PP, and the inner preposition contributes a relation while the outer one selects or adjusts it. *Out of the box* is not a wordier *outside the box*; it is *out* taking *of the box* as its complement. The recursion is syntactic, not a quirk of individual idioms.

*Notwithstanding the weather* and *the weather notwithstanding* show a preposition that may follow its complement. Head before complement is the norm, so the exceptions stand out. A different pattern appears in *spoonful by spoonful*, *day by day*, *piece by piece*, where a repeated form distributes a situation over time or quantity rather than locating it once.

sections.title: Stranding and the order of complement and head

blocks.text: *What was she referring to?* The preposition sits at the end, its complement has moved to the front, and the sentence is unremarkable. English does this constantly — in questions, relatives, exclamatives, comparatives, hollow clauses and passives — leaving the preposition behind and co-indexing the gap with the fronted phrase. Head before complement, as in *with pride*, is the default order, not the only possible one.

In some of those constructions the preposition can travel with its complement instead: *To whom are you speaking?*, *the article to which I referred*. This is pied-piping, and the choice between it and stranding is partly structural, partly a matter of register.

The old prohibition on ending a sentence with a preposition has no basis in the grammar. Stranding has been standard for centuries and is unremarkable in most registers. Fronting often sounds formal, and it sounds pedantic when the stranded version is what any speaker would say. What is at stake is a choice between constructions, not a verdict on correctness.

A handful of prepositions allow the complement before the head: *the weather notwithstanding* alongside *notwithstanding the weather*. The complement is still present, so this is not stranding; it is an alternative order inside the PP. Preposing a whole PP is a third phenomenon: *To your father I’m even more deeply indebted* moves preposition and complement together.

blocks.text: *For the sake of the children* has a recognisable shape and a meaning you cannot compute from its parts. *At odds with the evidence*, *on the grounds that the evidence is unreliable*, *up against a deadline*, *in brief*: each is headed by a preposition, each is more or less fixed, and none is fully predictable from the words inside it.

Fixed does not mean unstructured. *For the sake of* still takes a noun phrase complement; *on the grounds that* still takes a content clause; *at odds with* still takes a PP. The idiom is a lexical unit built out of ordinary syntax, which is why a complement can appear inside it and why a modifier can sometimes squeeze in without breaking it.

*In brief* and *of old* have petrified further. The element after the preposition looks adjectival, but there is no predicand for it and no reason to call it predicative; the phrase has hardened into a single unit. *What with* behaves differently again, introducing a reason adjunct and taking a coordination of PPs or clauses after it.

sections.title: What PPs do in larger constructions

blocks.text: *Rely on the evidence* and *before breakfast* both contain a PP, and only the first is required by the word it attaches to. Complements are licensed — by a verb, noun, adjective or preposition, as in *rely on*, *a reliance on*, *keen on*, *inside of*. Adjuncts such as *in the garden* or *with great care* attach to the clause and add information. One PP can be a complement in one clause and an adjunct in another.

Phrases also take PP modifiers: *proud of her* modifies an adjective, *independently of the result* an adverb, *the woman in the garden* a noun, *from behind the curtain* another PP. Some PPs stand outside the clause as supplements, as *In short, the plan failed* shows. A few can even be subjects — *From here to London is over fifty miles*.

Meaning does not settle the function. *On the table* is a complement in *The report is on the table* and an adjunct in *She read it on the table*, with the same preposition and the same kind of complement. What changes is what the verb requires: *be* needs the locative, *read* does not. Clause structure then decides whether the phrase counts as complement or adjunct.

blocks.text: *The plan was approved by the boss.* Nothing in *by* means “agent”; the passive puts it there. This is what it means for a preposition to be grammaticised: the construction selects it, and its contribution is relational rather than spatial or temporal. *Of* in *the destruction of the city*, *to* in *give it to Kim*, *with* in *pleased with the result* work the same way, as required markers rather than free lexical choices.

The passive *by* is the clearest case because the correspondence with the active is so tight. *By the boss* is the internalised version of the active subject, and the same *by* marks an agent inside a noun phrase — *the approval of the plan by the boss* — although the NP construction is not a passive clause with its pieces rearranged.

*Of* is the default linker between a noun or adjective and its complement: *the destruction of the city*, *proud of her achievements*. Where the head prefers something else, the preference is a lexical fact — *marriage to Pat*, *a ban on smoking*, *keen on opera*. There is no route from meaning to preposition here; the pattern has to be learned with the word.

Comparison grammaticises *as* and *than*, and *as* also heads predicative complements — *I regard her as my best friend*. *At*, *for*, *from*, *in*, *on* and *with* each carry clusters of grammaticised uses beside their spatial and temporal ones. The same preposition can be a free choice in one construction and a required marker in another.

blocks.text: *The pen is on the table.* Two entities, one relation: the pen is located, the table locates it. Cognitive semantics calls the located entity the trajector and the reference point the landmark, and the labels earn their keep once the relation stops being static, since a trajector can move from a source, along a path, to a goal.

English divides the basic spatial work among a small set of contrasts. *At* locates, *to* marks a goal, *from* marks a source; *on* pairs with *off* and *in* with *out*; *into* and *onto* mark goals while *off* and *out of* mark sources. *Away* can mark source with or without *from*, which is one reason the system is better handled as a set of oppositions than as a list of translations.

Time borrows the spatial vocabulary almost wholesale. *At three o’clock* marks a point, *on Monday* a day, *in July* a month, each with the preposition that suits its granularity. *Before the meeting* and *after lunch* use path relations; *since 2020* marks a source; *for two hours* marks extent. The mapping holds because time is construed as a line and situations as points or regions along it.

*Between* and *among* are not divided by number. *Between* treats the members individually, as boundary points; *among* treats them as a collective. Both *between the trees* and *among the trees* are grammatical, but *between my toes* is normal and *among my toes* is not, because toes present themselves as individual boundaries rather than as a mass.

blocks.text: *Who did you speak to?* or *To whom did you speak?* Both are grammatical; they belong to different registers. A writer who avoids stranding everywhere produces prose that feels stiff, and a writer who fronts without control sounds archaic. Choose according to the occasion, not according to a blanket rule.

Idioms need more care, because their meaning is not compositional. *For the sake of* is not a paraphrase of “for the reason of”; *at odds with* is not a spatial relation; *on the grounds that* carries a fixed evidential force. Change the preposition and the idiom changes, or collapses.

Preposition choice also encodes lexical patterns that a dictionary has to record. *Depend on*, *rely on*, *keen on*, *a reliance on* share a preposition because each head selects it. *Different from*, *different to* and *different than* vary by dialect and register. Meaning alone will not tell you which form a head takes.

blocks.text: Everything here follows from one move: a preposition heads a phrase. It takes complements of several categories, accepts modifiers, and can occur without one. The class includes many traditional subordinating conjunctions and a subset of traditional adverbs, and it is closed without being small.

PPs serve as complements, adjuncts, modifiers, supplements and, occasionally, subjects. Their complements range over NPs, PPs, AdvPs, AdjPs and clauses, and the object/predicative distinction applies inside the phrase. Stranding, pied-piping and the rare complement-before-head order are structural options, not errors.

Grammaticised prepositions — *by*, *of*, *to*, *with* — are selected by constructions and often behave like case markers. Spatial meanings extend into time and abstraction. Style is a matter of choosing the construction that fits the register, not of applying a blanket prohibition.

blocks.title: A PP checklist
blocks.text: Find the preposition and its complement. Decide whether the complement is an object, predicative, PP, AdvP or clause. Check for modifiers and nesting. Then identify the PP’s function in the larger construction: complement, adjunct, modifier or supplement.

options.feedback: Outside and since can head PPs without complements.

options.text: They always take an NP complement.
options.feedback: They can take PPs, AdvPs, AdjPs and clauses too.
Right under and two years after show modification.

worked: Take *The keys were left just inside the drawer, behind a pile of old photographs*. The main PP *just inside the drawer* is headed by *inside*, modified by *just* and complemented by *the drawer*. The second PP *behind a pile of old photographs* is an adjunct locating the keys relative to another landmark.

The example shows the layered structure of PPs: a head, a modifier, a complement and a nested NP. It also shows that a PP can function as an adjunct in clause structure without being predicated of the subject. The keys are not “behind” in any inherent sense; the PP merely locates them.
application: When you analyse a PP, find its head and complement first. Then decide whether any other expression is a modifier or a second complement. A nested PP such as from behind the curtain has its own head and complement inside the larger phrase.

Next, identify the PP’s function. Is it required by a verb, noun, adjective or preposition? Is it an adjunct, a modifier, a supplement or a subject? The same PP can have different functions in different clauses, and the function determines whether it is a complement or an adjunct.

Finally, consider order and register. Stranding is normal, fronting is often formal, and a few prepositions allow their complement to precede them. Idiomatic PPs have fixed internal patterns, and grammaticised prepositions are selected by the construction rather than chosen freely.
reveal: In *The keys were left just inside the drawer, behind a pile of old photographs*, *inside* heads the PP *just inside the drawer* and takes *the drawer* as its object. *Just* modifies that PP. *Behind a pile of old photographs* is a separate PP adjunct with *a pile of old photographs* as its complement.
recap: Prepositions are phrase heads and take a wide range of complements. The category includes clause-taking and intransitive prepositions, and excludes whether, interrogative if and clause-introducing that. PPs can be nested, modified and used in all major syntactic functions.

Stranding and pied-piping are both grammatical. Grammaticised prepositions mark grammatical relations, while spatial meanings extend into time and other domains. The main analytical task is to identify the head, complement and function of each PP.

self_check.question: Why are prepositions analysed as heads rather than as words that merely precede nouns?
self_check.answer: They take complements of several categories, can be modified, can occur without complements, and head phrases that function as complements, adjuncts and modifiers.

self_check.question: Which traditional subordinating conjunctions are excluded from the preposition category?
self_check.answer: Whether, interrogative if, and clause-introducing that are treated as subordinators.

self_check.question: What is the difference between stranding and pied-piping?
self_check.answer: Stranding leaves the preposition in place while its complement is fronted; pied-piping fronts the preposition together with its complement.

self_check.question: What is a grammaticised preposition?
self_check.answer: A preposition selected by a grammatical construction, such as by in a passive or of in a noun complement.

self_check.question: How do between and among differ?
self_check.answer: Between treats members individually or as boundary points; among treats them collectively.

options.feedback: It is not a free locative choice.
That is the ordinary locative meaning.
It takes the boss as complement.

closing.prompt: Why is between preferred in between my toes?

options.text: The toes are treated as individual boundary points.
options.feedback: Between construes the members individually.
The contrast is not a simple count.
Among is a preposition too.

predict.prompt: Which word heads the PP in the drawer?

options.feedback: In heads the PP and takes the drawer as object.
The drawer is the complement.
Drawer heads the NP complement.

guided.prompt: What kind of complement is behind the curtain in from behind the curtain?

options.feedback: Behind the curtain is a PP headed by behind.
The NP object is the curtain.
No clause is present.

transfer.prompt: Why is right under the bed evidence for a PP?

options.text: Right is a modifier restricted to prepositions.
options.feedback: It does not modify verbs, adjectives or adverbs in Standard English.
Here it modifies a PP.
It has the bed as complement.

exit.prompt: What is the difference between stranding and pied-piping?

options.text: Stranding leaves the preposition in place; pied-piping fronts it with its complement.
options.feedback: Both are grammatical constructions.

options.text: Stranding is ungrammatical; pied-piping is correct.
options.feedback: Both are grammatical.
It fronts the preposition along with its complement.
